On the question of national education, the
working men from the first took their stand
on the broader and more national ground,
away from the narrowness of sect and party.
They asked for a system that would apply
equitably, and without fear et favour to all.
They asked the State to use the national funds
only for the education of the citizens. The
Church, however, backed by respectable :and
pious imbecility, such as a crowd of old de-
feated voluntaryists supplied, cried out against
this, and the Government, afraid to trust to
the popular: judgment, made a miserable com-
promise on a question where the true policy
was as clear as the sun at noonday, and now
they are face to face With a danger which,
when the battle-trial comes, will smash them
like glass. Mr. GLAnSToNE must not, Cannot,
dare not, do what Cardinal CuntliN will 'de-

And if promises were given to purchase
support when the Liberal men of England '
were overborne in Parliament, the Govern.
ment must either disgracefully violate these,
or clear out. They have shamefully neg-
lected a plain duty by making a cowardly
compromise, and the penalty will have to be
paid. •
Public writers and speakers, including those
who manage the affairs of ;the" nation in
Parliament, must recognise- the .faet that
the most active and enterprising people
in the country belong to our great cities
and towns. Seventeen parliamentary boroughs
in England and Wales, net counting those
belonging to the metropolis; contain more
than one hundred thousand inhabitants
each. Everywhere in these there is growth,
activity, intellectual life, political thought, and
movement ; their public institutions, their
newspapers, the energy imparted by the busi-
ness of their lives, must neeessarily tell in the
settlement of all disputed questions against
the squires who bear sway over an intellectual
wilderness. The Church, if it means to re-

squires, if they would have their voices lis-

stupid calumnies against trades unionism,

men to whom they now address themselves as
teachers. The true relations of distributors
and consumers, and of producers and con-
sumers, are finding practical interpretation at
the hands of the co-operators of the kingdom.
The relationship of employers and. employed
becomes modified daily by the notion of trades'
unions. Common thoughts agitate the minds
of working-men all over the world, wherever
the press penetrates, and, where does it not find
its way at the present moment? The best
men amongst our thinkers place themselves
courageously on the side of the people; espe-
cially in England and America, where the
people trust to intellectual, moral, and legal
means for their progress.

articles.text:
POPULMt, POWER.

Arran the predictions uttered by so many
prophets of evil in regard to the growth of
popular power in the State, it is curious to
observe with what equanimity of temper and
cheerful confidence our public writers and
speakers seem to regard the future. Now,
and then, by way of variety, some faint cry
of alarm is raised, but these nearly always
originate in distrust of foreign Governments,
or foreign rivals in trade, and not from any
fear of an abuse of power on the part of the
masses of our working people. The "Battle
of forking" had no reference to an insurrec-
tionary movement on London, nor does the
Stupid outcry about "foreign competition"
pre-suppose disloyalty in the workshops of the
country. .
It may be said with truth that, as far as the
politioel action of our working .men is con..
corned, all. signs are hopeful and point to
peace, to national progress, and to a sound
'.equity in the management of the affairs
of the nation. It: is very much a
fashion on the part of certain public in-
struotors, especially those who are professors
of the "dismal science," to lecture working
men in "good set terms" on the absurdity of
their opinions and the mischievousness of
their tots. Mr. NEWMARCIT and others seem
quite indignant because men who work will
.not defer to them as thinkers. Ttheso
teachers will have to find out that they really
are not infallible, and that, presumptuous as it
may appear, those 'who Work have many justi-
fications for concluding that there is more
*atonal than reality in much, of what is
tittered by such persons. Whatever may be
said to the contrary, old idols arc losing their
power, eld faiths of all sorts arc dissolving,
and that more universal thought which springs
from a more universal culture and a wider
•exporionce, is moving the masses forward by
their own impulses. The power to drive
hem hither and thither, to hound them
or to draw them oil' by appeals to
their prejudices and passions, is becoming
perceptibly less, though it still unfortunately
exists.

Without making any reference to the
growth of Republicanism, which may or may
net he destined to take possession of the
future, it is certain that blind attachment to
classes and families is dying out. Neither the
BoußnoNs, the IlAranunos, or the Hou.E.N-
ZOLLE,B,NS can count on the unfailing loyalty of
their followers, whilst everywhere principles
relative to the business or life nationally and
internationally are taking possession of men's
minds and influencing more and more their eon-
duct. In thissenssit is that public opinion every
where is interfering to enforce sound and
just policies, and thwart the ambitious claims
of our great governing families. The masses

of the people are binning to see that how-
ever they may be aivided by seas, rivers, or
mountains, they have principles in common;
and that their common interests point to peace-
able and friendly intercourse.

That terrible war which troubled the early
portion of the present century was a battle of
dynasties, fighting to prevent the growth of
any but what they considered legitimate
power; and although the mad ambition of the
first BONAPAIITE drew the people of the dif-
ferent nations by their own will into it, and
to that extent popularised it, its originating
cause was hatred of popular sovereignty and
a determination to uphold Divine Right on the
part of the monarchs and statesmen of Europe.
Our aristocracy then acted in accordance with
their prejudices and interests as a class; such an
attempt in the present day would be their
destruction. Public opinion is so wedded to
higher and truer national policies, that if, under
any provocation, our aristocratic classes at-
tempted to move in such a direction their
grave would open under their feet. The
growth of the people'a power will not long
permit the lives, the property, and the hap-
piness of nations to be destroyed for the pas-
time or the aggrandisement of kings and
nobles, and this change in the thought
and temper .of the public in England will
most certainly, ere long, be brought home to
those who now gamble away the happiness of
the people on the Continent of Europe. Pain fnl
as the late American war was it brought out
.the fad, not only of the growth of popular
influence, iset it also made the wise and bene-
ficent spirit of that power plainly manifest.
An old institution, involving the degradation
Of men, devolving as an 'inheritance on a Re-
public, sustained by the rights of property,
and defended on the ground of interest, pre-
judice, and unjust law, was stricken down by
the righteous indignation of the masses of
the American people. On grounds of humanity,
right, and reason, the workers left the fields and
workshops, and moved by the highest impulses,
and by a policy as wise as it was self-sacri-
ficing, gave their lives for the preservation of
their grand Republic, and for the destruction
for ever of the degrading and disgraceful stigma
which 'marred its fair fame. Hero in England
the cause of American. slaveholders was
championed by our ruling classes, by
the men who claim the right of dictating
to, and directing our workers. The peace
of the wot chief nations of the world
were at risk in this strife. America would
have been ruined if broken into fragments on
this slave question. England might have
gone absolutely to wreck if she had been drawn
into war with America by Alabama builders
and Southern sympathisers, Lot it never be
forgotten that her working men saved her.
In spite of folly, and knavery, and class pre-
judice, they kept her hands clean from those
high offences against GOD and man, towards
the commission of which she was drifting.
The so-called respectable classes in the nation
disgraced her ; cotton bondholders, newspaper
editors, heaven-born statesmen, Alabama
builders stained her reputation, pawned her
honour; did, all men could to sink her in
infamy. But, lot it he repeated, her working
men, suffering supremely in consequence of
that abominable ell'ort to preserve and extend
the curse of slavery, stood firmly by principle
and kept the nation in the path of duty.

fifty-four per week. The meeting resolved to ad-
here to fifty-one hours as the limit of a full week's
Work, also the readjastment of °Verde e as sought,
and that the men should cease to work unless the
demand is coneeth4l,

The employers held a meeting on Saturday, wben
it was agreed That the whole subject in dispute
Should be referred to an arbiter, in order to arlii

the evils of a strike, which would be inevitable if
this proposal was not accepted. A letter to this
effect was sent to thg-men, who mot in the evening
to consider it. They refused to submit their case
to arbitration, because anything granted short of
what was demanded would not be accepted. They
were willing, however, that a conference of em-
ployers and delegates should be held, having for
its basis the question of 61 hours as a full week's
work. This answer has been returned to the em-
ployers.

A meeting of the employers was held on Tues-
day, when they agreed to the proposal of the men
to have a conference, but on the understanding
that by so agreeing their position was not in any way
compromised. They stated that they were quite
willing that the hours of labour be ruled by what
was determined in Glasgow.

articles.title: BIRMINGHAM
articles.text:
BIRMINGHAM

DIVISION OF rrtorrra AMONGST NVOIIKPEOI'LE.

The following circular has been issued by Mr,
J. S. Wright to the workpeople of the firm of
Smith and Wright, button manufacturers, Brearley.
street West, Birmingham :.••
"165, Brearley.street West,
"30th December, 1871.

" Mr. Smith having kindly given over to me the
principal part of the profits of the concern, I am
enabled to carry out a desire I have entertained
for many years, to lot those who work for me
partake of some.of the profits arising from their
labours.

"I have found it very difficult to divide, in a
satisfattory manner, the amount I have set aside
for that purpose; what I now give must not be
considered an exact apportionment to the value of
the service , rendered, but only a recognition of
the principle which I desire to act upon.

"In the present distribution I include, as nearly
as I can ascertain, all those who wero above
twenty-one on Ist lanuary, 1869, and who have
continued to work for me from that date.

" Tho amount is from the profits of tho year 1870.
It will give me groat pleasure if I can soo my way
to distribate as largo or a larger amount from the
profits of 1871.

"It. would be satisfactory to me if your weekly
earnings were larger; but these must be determined
by. the custoni , of the trade,, the competition to
which it is subject, and other circumstances over
which I can have no control.
"in conclusion, I hope that the sum which /
now hand you, and indeed all your earnings, will
be so expended as to give you comfort, promote
your independence, and contribute to the happi-
ness of yourself and all those who belong to you.
"Wishing you a, happy. New Year, and that you
may have the blessing of go 4 all through, this
life, and the life eternal ia the world to come, I
remain, yours truly,

it SOHN Sunnow WRIGHT."

The amount divided, we (Birmingham Post) are
informed, ranges from one pound each for women,
to three or four pounds, according to value, for
men employed by the firm—no doubt in all cases
forming an acceptable New Year's gift.

articles.title: SHOEING-SMITHS.
articles.text:
THE SHOEING-SMITHS.

A general meeting of operative shooing-smiths
was held on Saturday night, at the King's Arms,
rershore-street. Mr. Preeman, who presided, said
the object of the meeting was to petition the em-
ployers for an advance in the present rate of wages,
which, in proportion to the amount of work done
by them, was exceedingly small. One of the
workmen present said that in Manchester the fire-
men wore receiving from 28s. to 365., and the
doormen from 21 to 28s. por week ; while in Bir-
minghaui the firemen were only receiving from
245. to 2s. a week, and the doormen a guinea, and
yet had to work equally as hard as those in Man-
chester. After some discussion, it was resolved
that the employers be petitioned to advance the
wages of the doormen 35., and each class of fire-
men 2s. a week.

CONTEMPLATED STRUM AN:ONG TU2 IRON SPOON

FORGERS.

A meeting of the iron .spoon forgers of Birming-
ham was held on Wednesday night in the British
Workman to consider what steps should be taken
in reference to the refusal of the employers to
consent to the request of the men in reference to
the discontinuance by them of the payment of
shop-rent and tiring. ltr. James Mason presided.
Mr. li.iiodgkins proposed :—" That we, the iron-
spoon forgers, do not intend deviating from our
fornier preposition ; that is, to discontinue paying
shop-rent and tiring. Having given our employers
due and proper notice •on the former not
being discontinued, and after making several ap-
plications, the masters will not come to any satis-
factory conclusion with us."—The resolution was
unanimously carried,

WIGAN.
THZ COAL MINERS.

The miners of West Houghton, in connection
with the Wigan Miners' Benefit Society, cele-
brated their annual day on Saturday, December
30, at the Four Awls Inn, with a good substantial
dinner.

After, a public meeting was hold. A working minor
was in the chair, and after referring to tho bene-
fits and the advance of wages, the eight hours
movement, the Mines Bill, the Criminal Amend-
ment Act, &e., he called upon Mr. Wm. Aspinall,
one of the agents for the district, to address the
meeting, and after arguing the above objects for
40 minutes, the speaker resumed his seat amidst'
great applause.
On january Ist the minors of Skolmersdale, in
connection with the Wigan Miners' Provident
Benefit Society, celebrated their annual day at
their lodge room, at Mr. Walter Bimson's, Darby
Arms, by a public meeting, at 11 o'clock in the
morning. A working minor was in the chair, and
after a few remarks, he called upon Mr. Win.
Aspinall, the agent for the district, to address the
meeting.
The speaker, after giving the compliments of
the season, and wishing them all a Happy New
Year, reviewed the history of the Association from
1862 up to 1872, and in a telling discourse of
upwards of one hour, he said the good old Book
said there was a time for all things, so there was
a time for him to sit down.

Afterwards a procession was formed, headed by
the Skelmersdale Brass Band, and walked through
the village and back to the club-room, when the
members and their wives partook of a good dinner,
and the evening was spent in recreation, and
with the usual vote of thanks to all concerned.
The meeting was brought to a close after the
following resolutions were unanimously passed
by both the above meetings, which represented
over 1,000 men :-
I.—" That, in the opinion of this meeting, the
long hours worked by the miners of Laneashire are
injurious to the social, physiz‘,al, moral, intellec-
tual, and general condition of the miners, and this
meeting pledges itself to agitate the question till
eight hours out of the twenty-four be adopted in
the country generally."
2.—" That, in the opinion of this meeting, the
shuffling and shelving of the Mines Bill of late
years has been injurious to us as a mining popu-
lation, arid this meeting pledges itsolf to agitate
and assist all in our power to secure the passing of
a satisfactory Mines Regulation Bill early in the
coming session of Parliament."

3.—" That, in the opinion of this meeting, the
Criminal Amendment Act passed in 1871 is unjust
and uncalled for, and these two meetings pledge
themselves to use all their efforts to get the Act
repealed, and made just and satisfactory."

BANBURY.
THE NINE HOMO.

I am very sorry to inform you that the nine
hours movement is not takirlg quite so good a
turn as we should like. There is one firm (Messrs.
Barrow and Steward) that will not conform to
reasonable terms. They have conceded the nine
hours, but cannot agree as to how it shall be
worked. They have offered the men terms which
they cannot accept ; so the consequence is they
struck work on Monday, and they paid about fifty of
the men off on Tuesday, so it will be seen they
have very few left, except a few old men, the ap-
prentices, and the foremen in each department.
The men want the nine hours pure and simple—
that is, to leave off at five at night, but the masters
say they are determined to keep the shop open
and the machinery running till half-past five, and
want them to have longer meal times and five
minutes after six in the morning ; HO the time
would be very little good to them.

articles.title: STRIKE OP ENOINEP,ItB.
articles.text:
STRIKE OP ENOINEP,ItB.

On Monday a great number of men in the em-
ploy of Messrs. Barrows and Stewart, engineers,
Banbury, struck, in consequence of the firm
having refused to accede to the nine hours move-
ment. The building firms in the town have agreed
to a reduction of hours.

SOUTH STAFFORDSUIRE.

TUB COLLIERS AND TILE NINE moults' MOVEAIENT,

On Saturday night, a well-attended meeting of
colliers WAS held at the Limerick Inn, Great
Bridge, to consider what steps should be taken in
order to secure the adoption of the nine hours'
system in the collieries in the district.

The Chairman having advised those present to
be united in their action,
The following resolution was then moved,
seconded, and carried unanimously :—" That un-
less the masters adopt the nine hours' system at
the end of next week, fourteen days' notice be
given to play on Mondays And Thursdays."

DARLASTON.
TIM RUT-AND-BOLT MAXERS.

On Friday night a meeting of nut-and-bolt
makers was held at the Scott Arms Inn, Blackball,
Darlaston, to consider what steps should be taken
with regard to the list of prices that had been
prepared and forwarded to the men by their em-
ployers. Mr. Mark Ashey took the chair.
Mr. Jugging (tho Secretary) read a copy of the
list prioes that had been prepared by the masters,
which showed a very considerable reduction in the
prices quoted in the men's list—in one case a re-
duction as great as 6s. per gross.
Mr. John Hemmingsley then moved—
" That the list of prices received front the Em-
ployers' Association by the Nut and Bolt Makers'
Association be discountenanced and rejected with
contempt by this meeting."
Mr. Samuel Leman seconded the resolution,
which was unanimously carried:
Mr. John Gibbons moved—

"That the Secretary be empowered to inform
the Masters' Association that their list could not
be accepted."
Mr. Basnett seconded the motion, which was
also agreed to.

A further resolution, rejecting the rules of the
masters as well as their list of prices, was carried
unanimously. The meeting theft terminated.

articles.title: HUDDERSFIELD. THE WEAVERS' STRIKE.
articles.text:
HUDDERSFIELD.
THE WEAVERS' STRIKE.

The strike of weavers at Cliffe End Mills, near
nuddorsfleld, which has lasted five weeks, has
been amicably settled, the workmen having gained
an advanced scale of prices, payment In the middle
of the piece, and a holiday from one o'clock on
Saturdays.

SHEFFIELD.
TUB ENGINEEItS AND TILE NINE HOURS.

On Monday, about 600 men employed in the
engineering trades at the Cyclops and Atlas Works,
Sheffield, came out on strike, in consequence of the
conditions sought to be imposed by their employers
in the carrying out of the 5-1 hours movement.
Their example was followed by the engineers em-
ployed at three other largo works in the town.
The 54 hours movement was to have been gene-
rally adopted in Sheffield on Monday, but at the
works where the strike has occurred a difficulty
has arisen in consequence of the te?ms imposed by
the oMployors. A notice was posted on Saturday
informing the men that work was to commence at
half-past eight on Mondays, that an hour wqs to
be allowed for dinner, and that they were to leave
off at half-past five o'clock; that they were to
resume work at six o'clock all the other morn-
ings in the week, leaving off at half-past five
in the 'evening, and at half-past twelve on
Saturdays. With the usual meal times this would
make the required 51 hours. The notice
further states that overtime is to be paid thus—
the first four hours at the rate of time and a
quarter, and all beyond that limit at the rate of
time and a half; on Sundays the rate to be time
and three-quarters. The night-shift men are to
commence at six o'clock in the evening, and
work till six in the morning, with an hour and
half off for meals; five nights to constitute a week's
work; time and three-quarters for Sundays. The
tonne demanded by the men are these :-54 hours
to constitute a week's work in the day time, and
45 hours if worked at night; work to commence
at six o'clock in the morning all the year round,
and to cease at five in the evening, except on
Saturdays, when they shall leave at one o'clock.
Overtime to be paid-for at the rate of time and a
quarter for the first four consecutive hours, and
that if the men are required to work longer than
four hours, they shall be paid at the rate of time
and a half for the total number of hours worked ;
time and three-qu.%rters on Sundays. An inter-
view was held between deputations for the men
and their employers, but without a satisfactory
result.

THURSDAY.—The strike of the men at the Atlas
and elyclops Works, Sheffield, on the question of
detail in carrying out the nine hours movement,
has now come to an end. The masters have
granted the demands of the men, both with regard
to the arrangement of hours and the payment of
overtime. The workmen employed by Messrs.
Mark Firth's, Butcher's, and the Bessemer Steel
Works, are still " out " on the same question ; but
a settlement is soon expected.

The employes of John Brown and Co., and
Messrs. Calumet' have not struck. They have
simply requested permission to work the 54 hours on
a different principle from that which the employers
had laid down.

DUDLEY.

TUE COLLIERS AND TILE MORT TIME MOVEMENT.

At some of the collieries on the east and west
of Dudley notices wore given in by ihe ihinertion

JAN. 6, 1872.

Saturday. The notices were of a varied character,
some of them mentioning vaguely the nine hours
system, and others making the following different
requests, viz. :—" For two hours reduction," "one
hour reduction," "two hours reduction on Satur-
days only," and "two hours reduction with
increase of wages." The want of unity is mani-
fested by the circumstance that at some of the
collieries the " bandsmen " only seek a reduction
in the hours of labour, the pikemen remaining
satisfied. The divided councils render it highly
improbable that a general strike will take place;
indeed, the movement may be regarded as partial
and somewhat fictitious in its nature.

LEICESTER.
THE FRAME WORK XNITTERS..
On Monday, a large meeting of framework

knitters, representing the sock and top branches,
was held in the Temperance Hall, to consider a
list of advances proposed to be given from Mon-
day last, itt accordance with a resolution adopted
by a recent meeting of manufacturers and work- '
men before the board of arbitration and concilia-
tion. It was unanimously resolved that the advance,
which ranges from Is. to Is. 6d. per week, according
to the branch of labour, be accepted. Thus the
question of a strike has been averted, and the matter
of frame rents and charges stands adjourned for a
month. On the whole the arrangement is highly
satisfactory to the men.

TIIE STONEMASONS.
At Leicester, the master builders have received
notices for alterations of working hours and rules
from the stonemasons, bricklayers, and carpenters
and joiners, and the local association of masters,
which has lately been formed in this town, has
appointed a sub-committee to meet and confer
with the workmen in the hope of arriving at irn
amicable and permanent settlement of the matters.

articles.title: CINDERFORD.
articles.text:
CINDERFORD.

WAGES IN THE FOREST OF DEAN.

A meeting of colliers, miners, and mechanics
was held on Tuesday night at Cinderford for tho
purpose of deciding upon the terms of a circular to
be addrtssed to the coal and ironmasters of the
Forest of Dean. It was stated that, notwithstand-
ing the unprecedented advance both in coal and
iron, hundreds of the Forest of Dean miners war°
only paid from 17s. to 20s, a wock, whilst the
colliers employed by the Messrs. Crawshay were
'sly, with the October advance, receiving the same
rate of wages as given thou ton years ago, with
privileges equal to five per cont. knocked off. It
was resolved to demand that all coals should be
weighed on delivery at the pit's mouth ;
a five per
cent. advance to the day-men, end Iti per cent. to
the mechanics; the abolition of five-week pays ;
and the eight hour's system to the pitmen. The
meeting represented 5,000 colliers and miners.

COVENTRY.

THE CARPENTERS AND JOINERS.

Tbo motor builders of Coventry have re-
ceived the following notice from the joiners :
"Coventry, December 21, 1871.

" Gentlemen, —At a meeting of the Operative
Carpenters and Joiners, held at the Anchorlnn,West
Orobdard, Coventry, on Wednesday, December 13,
1871, it was unanimously agreed, that the delegates
chosen at the meeting give the masters three months
notice for an advance on their present rate of
wages, and that their wages in future be sixpence
-
halfpenny per hour, and all overtime made at
the request of the masters be paid for at the rate of
time and half, and for Sundays double time.
"W. RALPH, Corresponding Secretary,
"101, Spon-End."

articles.title: NOTTING HAM THE noxß MASONS.
articles.text:
NOTTING HAM
THE noxß MASONS.

At Nottingham, the builders have received
notioe from tho stonemasons that on and after May
Ist, 1872, the hours of labour shall be 60 per week
during summer, the time in winter to remain as at
present, and that there shall be an advance of
wages of one halfpenny per hour all the year
round.

NORWICH.
TUE BUILDING OPERATIVES.

The master builders have received the following
notice:

" 'rho Norwich United Building Association, hold
at 'The Farrier's Arms,' Pottergate-stroot, St.
John de Maddermarket.

"Sir,--After holding several meetings to discuss
the nine hours movement in all Its bearings, or
that 51 hours shall constitute a full week's work,
the association unanimously came to the conclusion
that on and after the first day of January, 1872,
that .54 hours shall constitute a full week's work,
and the time shall be as follows :—From 0.30
a.m. to 5.30 p.m., with one hour and a half for
meals for the first five days; and on SaturdaY

from 6 a.m. to 1 p.m., with half an hour for break-
fast. The advance of wages shall be one half-
penny per hour. To prevent the system of over-
time, sub-contracting, also jobbing work, &c.,
after the stated hours of labour, we shall be paid
time and a half. Having faith in this measure, we
consider it will prevent many relying upon paro-
chial relief. Therefore we one and all shall have
a better chance of work. No man shall be kept
more than one half-hour for payment after his
week's wolk is done. You arc requested to send
an answer on or before Wednesday, the 20th
December, 1871, to the above-named place."
(Signed by the Committee.)

articles.title: SHOEMAKERS.
articles.text:
THE SHOEMAKERS.

A large meeting of shoemakers in support of
the nine hours' movement was held at Norwich on
Wednesday night. It was stated that some of the
local firms engaged in the trade wore willing to
accede to the movement, but others were unwill-
ing to fall in with it. The men determined, how-
ever, to maintain a firm attitude upon the sub-

DEWSBURY.
AGITATION IN THE TRADES.

The doffin-plate makers of the Dewsbury
district have commenced an agitation for the nine
hours movement, and have by circular requested
"that they may be allowed the same privileges as
their follow-workmen, viz., to work nine hours
per day and receive 275. per week instead of their
present wages."
On Wednesday the whole of the men employed
in the machine, engineering, whitesmith, boiler
making, and other iron shops in Dewsbury,
Batley, Morley, and other portions of the Dewsbury
district commenced work on the nine hours system.
They have arranged with the employers to work
from six o'clock in the morning to five o'clock at
night. The masters wanted the time to be from
6.30 a.m. to 6.30 p.m.; but this arrangement the
men were not willing to accept, and the masters
made the concession.

BRISTOL.
TIIE BTONTIEASONB.

At Bristol the operative stonemason;' society
have given the master builders notice of altera-
tions in the existing trade rules, to come into
operation on the first of July next. The masons
want to wotk fifty-two hours a week in summer,
and forty-eight-and-a-half hours in winter. They
wish to be paid by the day, at their present rate
of 30s. a week in summer, and 28s. a week in
winter.

articles.title: MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.
articles.text:
MISCELLANEOUS TRADES NEWS.

The nail-forgers in the Dudley and Brotnsgrove
districts have agreed to give notice to the nail
masters for an advance of 10 per cent. on what
are known as "thousand " nails, with the alterna-
tive of a general strike unless the demand is
conceded on the first " weigh-day "in 1872.
The awl-blade makers at Bloxwich, near Wall.
sail, have decided to give notice for an ad-
vance of 10 per cent., and to leave work unless the
demand is conceded within 14 days.
The Willenhall locksmiths, at a meeting held on
Thursday night, passed a resolution pledging
themselves to take "all legal steps" with the view
of securing an advance of 10 per cent, on the
present rate of wages in all branches of the trade.

Mr. William Smith, Cavendish Engineoring
Works, Wells-streat, Oxford-stroot, has granted
the nine hours concession, thus making fifty-four
hours per week instead of sixty.
On Monday the Dewsbury Town Council ad-
vanced the wages of the police force as follows :
Superintendent, from £llO to £l2O per annum;
sergeants from 255, Cd. per week to 275. 6d. ;
first-class constables from 235. to 25.; and
second-class constables from 21s. to 235. ; per
week.

We hear that Messrs. E. Ripley and Son,
Bowling Dye 'Works, Bradford, have decided,
without solicitation, to adopt the nine-hours-a-
day system at their works in the course of not
month.

CELEBRATION OF THE NINE
HOURS.

In nearly all the towns throughout the country
the nine hours as a day's work came into opera-
tion on Monday, and the event has been cele-
brated by the workmen by process ions through
the towns with bands and banners.

Yonx.—On Monday the workmen in the employ
of the North-Eastern Railway Company at York
celebrated the inauguration of the nine hours
movement by a procession, in which they were
joined by workmen from other firms to whom the
boon had been conceded. The procession
was on a scale hitherto unequalled in York. The
procession was conducted in the most orderly
manner, and both at its commencement and
during its progress cannon were fired in honour of
the occasion. After the procession an address
was read on behalf of the workmen, in which they
said they took that opportunity of placing on
record their grateful sense of the conciliatory
spirit which has prompted the several large
employers of York to concede the great boon
involved in the limitation of the hours of labour
to nine hours per day.

BLACKBURN.—On Monday 600 ironworkers
walked in procession through the main streets of
Blackburn to celebrate the adoption of the nine
hours system in all the foundries of Blackburn.
The procession was headed by a military band,
and on returning to the Town Hall some addresses
were delivered. A special resolution was also
passed thanking the employora for their generous
concession of 64 hours per week. Cheers wore
given for the employers and for the nine hours.

'BRIDGEWATER.-A great demonstration of work-
men in celebration of the adoption of the nine
hours movement by the principal employers of
labour in Bridgewater was held on Sunday night.
Upwards of a thousand workmen, carrying
torches, transparencies, and trade devices, formed
a procession, accompanied by three bands.

NIWCASTLE.—A :air de was hold in the Town
Hall on Monday night to inaugurate the nine
hours system, which has just come:into operation
in the North. Mr. Joseph Cowan, jun., presided.
He pointed oat lessons which the late strike
should teach both employers and artisans, The
former ought not to miscalculate the strength of
their opponents, but to treat their requests with
courtesy and respect. The men ought to organise
and prepare for other struggles, should they
unhappily arise. Mr. Burnett, the President of
the Nino Hours League, and other delegates,
spoke. Mr. Burnett predicted that the time WftB
coming sooner or later when eight hours would be
recognised a day's work, and urged the work-
men especially to give their attention to technical
education.

Irswrmr.—An entertainment of a novel character
took place on Monday evening, the leading
members of two Ipswich mechanical firms, Messrs.
Ransomes and Rapier, and Messrs. E. R. and P.
Turner, being invited to dinner by their work -
people to celebrate the concession of the nine
hours :movement. An address to both firms was
presented by the men, and the evening was spent
in the most harmonious manner.

DONCISTEIt.-A short time ago the Great
Northern Railway Company conceded to their
employds lit the Plant Works at Doncaster a re-
duction in the hours of labour, in conformity with
the nine hours scale, which has become so general
in the country. The new arrangement comes into
operation with the commencement of the year,
and by way of marking the occasion in a suitable
manner, the skilled artisan's, forming the Don-
caster branch of the Amalgamated Society of En-
gineers, dined together on Tuesday afternoon at
the Black Bull Inn. Mr. Councillor A. 3. Smith
(the ex-Mayor) occupied the chair, and amongst
other visitors wore Dr. Dunn, Dr. C. Wilson, and
Mr. Councillor Goldert. Some speeches were
made after dinner, remarkable alike for their good
sense and the loyal, patriotic sentiments expressed.
It was asserted, amidst much applause, that a
trade unionist did not imply that tho man was a
Communist or a member of the International.
The principles of men and movements such as
those mentioned had no sympathy from the
speakers, and trade outrages were strongly con-
demned. A hope was expressed that the nine
hours movement might prove beneficial alike to
employers and employed.

TYNEsinu.—The nine hours day's work was com-
menced on Tuesday, as 4 rule, in all the engine

works on Tyneside. Nominally it cane into
operation on New Year's Day, but few or any of
the factories resumed full work until Tuesday. In
addition to the engine factories nearly all the
large works in Northumberland and Durham,
employing artisans, commenced with the nine
hours on New Year's Day, which may now be
considered as the standard of tie day's work in this
part of the country.

&urn WALES.—The leading establishments of
South Wales are one by one adopting the nine
hours system. The Llanolly Railway and Dock
Company, the Swansea Vale Railway Company,
and the Rhymney Railway Company have algal.
fled their intention of reducing the hours of labour
to nine per day, and memorials from the men are
now before the directors of the Taff Vale, the
Great Western, and several other companies.

CARDIFF.—The ironfoundera of Newport and

articles.text:
REFUSAL TO PAY UNNECESSARY

TAXATION.

Stn,.—May I ask you to insert the following
letter, which I have addressed to Mr. Lowo, the
Chancellor of the Exchequer P—l am, &c.,
Sr. &WITHIN WILLIAMS.

"To TUE RIGHT HON. THE CHANCELLOR OF

't THE ExonEQUEIL

"Sir,—lt is my deliberate intention not to pay
the income tax. In a humble way, I shall do
what Hampden did about the Ship Money; I shall
take care not to break your laws, but within the
limits of your laws I shall withstand you to the
utmost:

"I refuse to pay your demand for the same
reason that I should resist the demands of a high-
wayman or a burglar. Archbishop Whately re-
minds us, that it is only so far forth as the taxa-
tion of a country is a fair charge for the services
rendered by the Government that taxation differs
from avowed robbery. Now, is forty-three mil-
lions a year a fair charge for the services ren-
dered to us by the tax consumers? Every ono
knows that all the real good you do for us could be
done for very much less than forty-three millions a
year. This is admitted by every Minister when out
of office. My own conviction is that twenty
millions a year of your taxation is unnecessary:
to that extent your taxation is robbery.

"In return for shameless taxation, you fail to
perform the first duties of a Government. So
ignorant are you of the art of war, that ten
thousand British soldiers, when lod by you, are no
match for a handful of Maori barbarians. You
cannot even tether our troop horses. Our seamen
you run aground and drown. Hundreds of
thousands of labour's hard earnings you fling into
the waves at Alderney; but our commercial ports,
on whose safety our food depends, you leave, with
sinister design, open to bombardment. Your
miserable allowance to witnesses and prosecutors
in courts of justice compels policemen, and all pru-
dent men, to shut their eyes when crime is com-
mitted. In order to check the growing wealth
and power of the industrial and commercial
classes, you contrive insolvency and bankruptcy
laws which have enabled the extravagant and dis-
honest to defraud the industrious and thrifty of
thousands of millions.

" It is not because it is the income tax that I
refuse to pay you. I wish that I could raise tho
issue on some tux still more iniquitous: such as
the millions you snatch from poor people's macs-
swims, their tea or sugar. As I neither import
nor make taxed articles I can challenge you only
on a direct tax. "

"Nor do I whit to shirk my duties as a citizen;
quite the contrary. When the Crireean war had
proved to us the imbecility of your standing arma-
ments, I was one of the first to become a volunteer,
a volunteer in earnest. If I save this income tax
from your clutches, I shall offer it as a donation
to societies for promoting political reform: the
'Pinancial efortn Association, the Liberation
Society, the Representative Reform Associa-
tion, &c.

"Your fallacy that if I pay you less some one
olso must pay you more, deceives no one who
understands your oxpendituro ; you just squander
all that you can lay your hands on. True, you
apply a little, now and then, to a sham reduction
of the nstional debt; but you run us into debt
again at the first opportunity; so that our national
debt is about as much to-day as it was forty years
ago. Could you rob us of another ten millions a
a year you would govern us no better; you dare
not rule us worse, if we saved twenty millions a
year from your bottomless pit.

"Until members who are, or have .been, tax
consumers, or whose fathers, sons, or sons-in-law
are tax ,consumers, are excluded from foting' on
questions of taxation, it is absurd to look t,)
liament for a reduction of taxation. For you
make it the interest (pecuniary or social) of a
majority in both houses to increase the expendi-
ture. A national refusal to pay unneaessary
taxation' is our only remedy; and it is a sure
one. You tried to tax our American bretherh
against their will, and you failed. The Irish,
peasantry got rid of your church ass and your
tenants' tithes by dogged non-payment. A few
Dissenters steadfastly refused to pay your church
rates, and church rates had to ho abolished. Your
can rob us of our chairs Lind tables, but they will
be of no use to you if we will not buy them of
you.

Ir. the hope that others may be induced to
follow my example, I shall publish this letter.
+II have the honour to be, Sir,
" 'lour faithful serrant,
"BT, fiWtrutx

" Oxford."

IMPORTANT NOTICE TO TRADES'

MIRTH ANNUAL CONGRESS OF
TRADES' SOCIETIES AND TRADES'
COUNCILS,

Ficuow Wonintsx —At the last Congress in
London it was agreed that the next Congress
should be held at Nottingham, commencing on the
Bth of January, 1872. One of the reasons for
meeting at that period of the year being that
questions affecting us, as Trades' Unionists and
Working Men, should be discussed immediately
prior to the assembling of Parliament, so that steps
might be taken towards combined action upon any
contemplated legislation by Parliament (or from
the Congress), on subjects having particular refer.
ewe to the working classes, without the introduc-
tion of party-political feeling.
It baying been deemed essentially requisite that
the last Congress should meet at a time when its
views could be made known on the Trades' Union
Bill before Parliament, and, notwithstanding the
strenuous opposition of the Congress to the
greater portion of the Bill, its objectionable
features have been retained in one half of the
original, under the title of the "Criminal Law
Amendment (Violence, Threats, &c.,) Bill," and
made extremely obnoxious by being specially
applicable to us as Trades' Unionists, pre-supposing
as it does criminal intentions on our part. The
class nature of such legislation, with a view to
its repeal or material modification must form a
prominent part in the proceedings of the Congress,
and we must not rest until the complexion of the
Bills is so changed that the authors of them will
recognise but little of the original. To accomplish
this object it should be the paramount duty of
every Trades' Society throughout the country,
whether affiliated or not, to be represented at the
Congress, so that greater force may be given to its
decisions.

The other subjects in the programme (some of
which have not heretofore been discussed) will,
it is hoped, not only tend to dispel some of the
erroneous ideas entertained respecting the action
of Trades' Societies, and notably so at the meeting
of the Social Science Congress, but will elevate
the future of labour, and show to those who are
apt to take a one-sided view, that Unionists of
the working classes can discuss, and are favour-
able to the adoption or any plan calculated to
promote their moral and social well-being.

Societies or members will use their own judg-
ment whether to introduce or forward papers or
propositions on the subjects mentioned. No delo-
gato will be allowed to read more than one paper
during the sitting of the Congress, and the time in
no case should exceed twenty minutes.

It is respectfully relocated that Trades' Councils
and Trades' Societies intending to be represented,
will notify the same to the Secretary before the
11th day of December, together with the subject
of the paper or proposition they wish to submit
to the Congress, and also that arrangements may
be made for their accommodation.

SATURDAY, JANUARY 6, 1872.

NINE HOURS AS A DAY'S NMI.

Iv will be seen by the notices we print else-
where, that in the various localities where the
nine hours movement has been successful
great rejoicings have,
taken place; and fora
other quarters, where it is still undeoided,
the reports of progress are so cheering that WO
are in hourly expectation of the news of vie"
tory on the part of the men. No rejoicing,
however extravagant, can be regarded AS all
exaggeration of the feeling which ought to
accompany such a triumph. It is not too
much to say that this nine hours success
may be regarded as a new starting point ill
the history of labour in England. Imme-
diately, it is equivalent to the reduction in
hands of some hundreds of thousands of men,
and in that way is an important enhancement
of the value of labour. What effect this maY
have on the trade of the country we do not wish
even to glance at. To us, so far as the work-
ing man is concerned, it has a meaning quiW
beyond this, and, when properly understood, of
a far higher kind.
The working classes have never yet tried
to discover what modification machinery
has wrought in their relationship to their
work. A vast mechanical working power
is growing up side by side with our
human workers, in comparison to which they
are but as units to thousands; whilst this
enormous producing power, daily increasing,
instead of relieving the working men of a
portion af the burden of their toil
under the direction of capital, has a ten-
dency to increase it, and make it more
galling. The working men, by taking their
stand on the nine hours working day,
practically demand an overhauling of the old
idea—actually insist that their position shall

hare its full consideration, and that the new
mechanical forces coming into operation shall
be turned in the direction of their welfare, as
well as in that of the capitalist, or of ani,
other class of society.

Our operative classes do not mean the injury
or destruction of any interest. They have no
desire that capital shall be diminished, or that
its owners shall suffer; but they will insist
that their condition, as men, shall not be over-
looked or disregarded—that they must be
partakers in the civilisation of the age, that
no set of doctrinaires shall set up rules of
conduct to them to be passively accepted,
though they
,direetly imply their social degra-
dation. ,

We shall now have many questions, which
our political economists considered settled, re-
opened, and we shall not consider the nine
hours day even as a final settlement of
that point. The BEE-HIVE came into life to
fight this battle, as one of its leading ob-
jects. We therefore rejoice in its attainment.
The victory may now be considered as
practically won, but our task is by no
means ended. Every point gained only opens
up new ground, and upon this the working
men are quite prepared to enter. The Congress
about to assemble at Nottingham will indicate
certain portions of this new work, and as
the organ of the working-men of Eng-
land, we shall enter on it with no mis-
giving as to the final result.

articles.title: CARDWELL AND HARCOURT AT OXFORD.
articles.text:
CARDWELL AND HARCOURT AT
OXFORD.

Tula tone of Mr. VERNON HARCOURT'S New
Year's speech at Oxford was at the outset
nearly as complimentary to his Right Honour-
able colleague and to the Government, as if ho
had enjoyed the opportunity of declining the
offer of the Solicitor-Generalship hi Mr
JEWEL'S favour. There was also a Downing-
streetish, flavour about the terms in which ho
adduced the national sympathy with the
Royal Family as a proof positive of absolute
contentment with existing institutions. While,
however, he thought that, if nothing but good
was to be spoken of the dead and gone, last
year's Session would have a short epitaph, he
adducedone of the two measures carried in it, the
abolition of 'University Tests, as "bearing the
sterling Mint stamp of a Liberal policy." With
this mention of a Bill forced upon the Govern-
ment by that portion of its party least satisfied
with its conduct on the subject of general
education, he joined something more than an
insinuation that the reason why the party,
being in a confessed majority, had not accom-
plished more results, was that it had not been
well-handled by its leaders, that, in fact, the
Government is less strong than its supporters
are.

The principles on which the compact be-
tween them was formed in 1868 were public
economy and religious equality. The failure
of the high contracting party (the men in
office) in the first point, Mr. HARCOURT attri-
buted, it seemed, mainly to the loss of Mr.
BRIGHTIB help—" a man whose great genius
had never been employed except for the
publio good." He (Mr. BRIGHT) himself
declared, while still a Minister, that, so long
as seventy millions a year arc exacted
from the industry of the people, in the
shape of revenue, no power on earth can
lift up the downprest masses from their snar-
ing condition. Under this very Government
the revenue, though at first reduced, had
risen again to between two and three millions
more than Mr. BRIGHT affirmed as a point
Within which any Ministry must confine itself
to merit confidence and support. In 1851,
our expenditure was but fifty-five millions; an
increase, therefore, of more than twenty
millions, with nothing to show for it in any
department or quarter; no, not even in educa-
tion yet. We must, therefore, have equal
measure meted out to all sorts of people, and
thus arrest the descent of the nation into the
bottomless pit of ever-increasing extravagance.

The Government must reform their own
outlay as effectually at least as they rid that
of those who proceeded them. That would
be one way of recovering lost influence over
their Parliamentary supporters.
On the subject of religious equality, or, as
lie preferred calling it, "political justice,'

Mr. HAttcotrirr reserved himself, content for
the present with branding the affected call
for purely social questions as the unfailing
symptom of a used-up party and a played-
out Administration. Any set of men might
hold office and take pay on the principle of
doing_ little and spending much. What is
wanted, Mr. lancounT ended by saying, is a
Ministry and a House of Commons to act upon
such information as that contained, concerning
the condition of agricultural labour, in the
present Bishop of MANCHESTER'S report, and to
square the tenure of land to the just claims of
those who live, or rather starve upon it.
Mr. CARDWELL, in his yearly speech at Ox-
ford, begankwith such topics as the PRINCE or
WAVES, education, temperance, and the
licensing law. What he wanted to urge upon
consideration was—that the Government and
Legislature are but the representatives of the
entire community, and can only not as the
' agents of the community; and, therefore, to
arm the Government and Parliament with
power to accomplish successfully great results,
there must be not only energy and vigour on
the part of the Government and the Parlia-
ment, but also the utmost disposition to merge
minor differences; in short, a universal spirit
of forbearance and conciliation. Arrived at
the Ist of January, he hopes we have loft be-
hind us the controversies of a former year.
He took credit to himself, however, as having
both reformed the Army, and aided to abolish
University Tests. The bulk of his speech
amounted to nothing; nor did he refer to the
prosperity of trade, and the buoyancy of the
revenue, like a man, who, with his colleagues,
was cherishing any large scheme of retrench-
ment, but had nothing to promise but "social
improvements."

articles.title: NEW PARLIAMENTARY DIFFICULTY.
articles.text:
A NEW PARLIAMENTARY DIFFI-
CULTY.

A NEW difficulty has arisen in connection
with the business of the House of Commons.
It is pointed at by the Saturday _Review,
and with so high an authority we may take
the matter for granted. It was suggested
in consequence of the resignation of tho
Speakorship by Mr. DayrsoN, and the many
considerations that crowd on the mind in con-
nection with the appointment of a successor.
"The present House of Commons," observes
our contemporary, " consists of wealthy and
respectable members, but some of them have
not originally belonged to the highest ranks of
society, and it is highly probable that succeed-
ing elections may lower the social standard
which has hitherto formed an almost indispen-
sable qualification for parliamentary life. The
EiPEAKEIL may have to deal with troublesome
demagogues, who will not be hampered
by the unconscious restraints of education
and manner." We see the difficulty
and feel the necessity of providing for it. And
if we may be allowed to aid in its removal, we
would suggest that there are two methods by
which it might be met. The first is, that a
person belonging to the very " highest
ranks of society" should be chosen, that there
might be no question about his instincts as a
gentleman; that, in addition, be should be in
the prime of life, six feet high at least, with
broad shoulders, loud voice, and altogether
with a sufficiently commanding and threaten-
ing manner to overawe the turbulent dema-
gogues who may be sent into the House by
the working-men. Should this be regarded as
insufficient, provision might be made for two
speakers, one from the "highest ranks of
society" and one from the lowest. Tho Editor
of Bell's Life might be able to suggest a &per-
son who could be returned for some Government
borough, and who should be thoroughly prac-
tised in the art of self-defence. Some respect-
able,retirod pugilist,who,instead of calling a vul-
gar demagogue to order, might, upon a hint frorn
his official brother of the "highest rank," walk
up to an offending member and bring him to
his seat by a flush hit on the nose, or by send-
ing his maulyvigorously into the "victualling
department" of the offender. Our respectable
contemporary will, we hope, take heart; where
there's a will there's a way. We must have
order preserved in the House of Com-
mons, and if knocking a man down is not
constitutional at present, we are fast going
in the direction to mac) it so. There are

friends of the Constitution at Bolton and
Reading who might be usefully consulted on
this rather puzzling subject, in anticipation of
the calamity hinted at by the Saturday
Review.

articles.title: PERSONS IN FRANCE.
articles.text:
PERSONS IN FRANCE.

THE PRESIDENT of the FRENCII REPUBLIC
has got over New Year's Day with well-acted
democratic modesty. He made no speeches to
his visitors, but simply shook hands. The
ORLEANS PRINCES were not observed among
those who paid their respects to him. The
Daats is the only journal of eminence that
seems to favour their dynastic pretensions, and
that but negatively. "Those," it says, in
reference to their having taken their seats in
the Assembly, "who give .their opinion on
affairs of State by speeches and open votes,
cannot surprise the national will." Free debate
is not the way to mako coups (Pella. There is
much meaning, however, in the election to
the French Academy of the Duke of AIIIIALE,
who had twenty -seven votes out of twenty-
eight, ten votes more than were given to
any ono of theother three successful candidates.
Another of these elections looked, perhaps,
in the same direction, that of the philo-
sopher LITTRE ; and that in its consequence
still more than in the fact itself ; the
consquence being that the Legitimist Bishop
of ORLEANS, in disgust at such a choice, re-
signed his own chair in the Academy. Per-
haps, however, the most significant circum-
stance of all is, that M. TRIERS may be
assumed to have voted for both the Duke
and the philosopher. Ho might say that ho
voted in both cases as one literary man for two
other literary men, which is no doubt true;
but it is impossible to avoid giving a politica
significance to elections in which such persons
are the voters, and such the candidates. It is
well known to have been the cherished ambi-
tion of the ex-EstrEnon to got in to the
Academy; but he was never able to command
the necessary amount of support among its
members, all his " works" notwithstanding.
The French Academy, it may be of use to
say, was formed in 1635 by the notorious
Cardinal RICIIELIEU, for the purification, re-
gulation, and general improvement of the
language of France. In 1691 it published its
famous Dictionary, which received many
additions in several reprints. The original
number of the members,of tho Academy was
forty. In 1793 it was abolished by the Revolu-
tion, but was afterwards restored as a branch
of the Institute of France. It now meets
twice a week, and vacancies in it arc filled
by the votes of the members, subject to
approval by "the Chief of the State," which
now means one of its most distinguished
members, M. TIIIEB.S. It is supposed always
to consist of the forty highest literary characters
in France.

THE PERMISSIVE BILL.

By order of the executive council of the
United Kingdom Alliance, the Alliance News
publishes an analysis of what is known as: the
Permissive Bill, which applies to all the three
kingdoms, and adds :—'The Bill does: not
touch the question of the licensing authority,
Snd the Alliance gives no opinion as to the
best method of granting licenses. The great
measure, for which nearly a million persons

may dispense the licences they shall not be
thrust into or perpetuated in any district
against the will of the inhabitants. The 13ill
provides the machinery for getting the public

certain point, the Bill declares that it shall be
potent, and the parish or district is then placed
An the circumstances as regards the -liquor
traffic which are to be found in nearly two

articles.title: COSTLINESS OF A REPUBLIC.
articles.text:
COSTLINESS OF A REPUBLIC.

Much has been said lately about the ex-
pense of royalty in England. Of the continental
republics the less said the better in connection
with national wealth ; but taking the United
States for comparison, the loss: of. time and
labour, the disturbance of trade and commerce,
and the unsettlement of business and credit
caused by each presidential election; outweighs
tenfold the cost of any monarchy. ' Were it
only for the saving to the nation by the quiet
constitutional mode in which a change of
government is effected, the superiority of the
English system is apparent. Ours is in fact
truer republic than theirs. A republic is
"a government by the people and for the
people." Ours is a monarchy only in name,
not an autocracy. The Queen reigns but does
not govern. She has far less political power
than the chief magistrate of the United States.
The President is . Comtnander-in-Chief of
the army and navy, and can order them where
he pleases, whether that makes war or not.
He nominates all the chief officers of the Go-
vernment, and the whole executive power is
vested in him. In . contrasting the two
Governments, the real comparison should be
between their President and, our Premier. A
vote of the House of Commons, expressing the
popular voice, can control or displace the Go-
vernment, which is not the case in America. It
is an admitted disadvantage, too, in the United.
States, that at every change of Government
the whole administration of the country, from
ambassadors down to village postmasters, may
have to vacate their posts. The change affects
the position and income of hundreds of thou-
sands of the population. The effect is that no
sooner is one Government established, than
agitation and plotting commence for the next
term of office. The judges of the Supreme
Court alone , are free from • this perpetual
political agitation. I never mot an American,
not a plaeeman, or aspiring to be a placeman,
who did not acknowledge the fault of this
Part of their system.—" Across the. Ferry; or,
First impressions of America." By the Editor
of the "..LeisureWour." (Ilodder and Stough-
ton).

The Manchester Courier says that in con-

opinion of some members that the police had

articles.text:
CAPITAL AND LABOUR.
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.

Slll,—After an abgenee, on looking over the
back files of theBEE-HIVE, I do not see that Mr.
Christopher Novae has taken any notice of
my question in, the case of the two persons, A
and B, on a desert island, having nothing but
what A 'saves of his share of the crop of
barley—" What 'ought to be the limit of A's
price, should he demand anything, in lending
to B some of his barley—his capital ?"
When out of the range of • the " higgling
of the market,"—a most prolific source of mfs.
representation, lying, fraud, theft, and
murder—the question would puzzle most per-
sons. Before answering it, taking a general
survey of what the working people of Eng-
land are doing, what do we see? They slave
away to obtain gold and silver from other
countries, which, as soon as got, is scattered
abroad in the shape ofloans for various purposes,
to be afterwards again gathered together, and
all the while poverty and ,misery frightfully
prevailing throughout the land. International
trade between countries of the same clime,
except on an extremely limited scale, is a very
great folly, as it unnecessarily throws away a
!•Vast amount of labour. This will be perceived
•: on the proper, legitimate, and just reward of
, labour being, understood.,
, Let us look into a little world—a school of
boys brought up in honest and truthful ways,
uncontaminated by trading as practised in the
commercial world. When, among themselves,
. one is desirous of selling, and another of buy-
an article—a knife for instance—how do
they arrive at the price of it? The first ideas
, which suggest themselves are, what did it
cost? and if the knife be as good, as new, that
is the price asked and paid without hesitation.
Should. it be the worse for wear, an estimate
and an allowance is made. No thoughts arise
to discover how keenly the seller is desirous
. of selling, or the buyer of buying, to be taken
advantage of; and no thoughts arise of making
a proilt—of getting something more than what
the article :cost. ,Should there be one who,
taking advantage-of .the buyer's ignorance, or
his desire for the article, asked; and, obtained
more than the cost price, all his companions,
on hearing it,
‘instinctively would cry -out,
Shame,!

A case may arise where ahoy might legiti-
mately ask more than the cost price, where,
for instance, he much valued a particular
picture in his possession, and another desired
to obtain it. The cost price would be no con-
sideration to overcome his repugnance to
parting with it, but he may do so on receiving
an offer, which he prefers to retaining his
picture. But the principle on which this sale
is effected is very different to the prevailing
one—which is, to discover the purchaser's
means, and bow much he desires the article,
and then charge the utmost they will bear.
One saves his pocket-money, and another
wanting it borrows it. It is lent without a
single thought of a charge, as the owner
knows when wanted it will be forthcoming.
Should he, at the time his friend asked for it,
*ant it himself, he might still be induced to
lend it by his friend offering something that
would overcome his repugnance to parting
with it—something that would be an equivalent
to the cost of the sacrifice made. '

A boy requires something to be done for
him; whom does he seek out to do it? Know-
ing that he lays himself under an obligation,
he seeks out him who can do it with the
greatest facility and in the shortest time.
He feels his obligation would be less than had
he employed one who, though as industrious,
would have taken double the time. And
what does he who performs the service expect
in return P Nothing more than the same tune
of equally laborious service. The thought
does not occur, because anyone else would
have taken double the time, that therefore he
might lay the receiver under an obligation for
that length of time. He regards simply his
time and trouble, his repugnance overcome in
the performance of the work, as the only basis
for a return.
In all these transactions each instinctively
felt that the equitable or natural measure of
price wet the cost, that is, -the amount of
money given, labour endured, sacrifice made,
in short, repugnance overcome. Had the
_idea for a moment arisen in the minds of
anyone of ascertaining what the value or
worth of the service or article was to the
receiver, he would naturally have felt it did
not concern him, he was meddling with the
other's affairs' and that it was extremely
impertinent to do so.
Cost, it will be perceived, has a positive
and negative aspect. It inoludes—(l) Active
performance of labour; (2) passive suffering,
, sacrifice, deprivation or endurance. Revert-
ing now to the question respecting A's price
in lending to B his barley, his capital, did A
act on the present commercial game and grab

system, he would squeeze B so as to make
him a slave as long as he could; but assuming
that he is a simple-minded, honest man under
the passive aspect of cost only could he
charge in lending; and his charge would be
the price for the surrender of the use of his
barley when it would be advantageous to him
to use it himself, but the exact measure of
the
_price of such surrender is the amount of
that sacrifice—not the amount of benefit
which he would confer on B by making it.
Petworth, Torquay.

THE LEGISLA.TIVE COUNCIL,
To the Editor of the BEE-Hivm.

'SIR,—As a working man, will you permit
me to make a few remarks upon an article
whieh appeared in your journal under the
above 'heading last week, by Rigby Wason.
The writer of .the article is evidently much
dissatisfied with the manner in which Mr.
Gladstone endeavoured to clear himself of the
many charges of blunders brought against
him. Your correspondent, after accusing Mr.
Gladstone of .sneering, goes on to say that he
was not surprised to read, "when he (Mr.
Gladstone) even out-Heroded Herod, in the
Absurdity of his defence against the grave
charge brought against him of having dis-
missed workmen for the low, 'dirty purpose of
cutting down his own estimates.". I had the
honour of hearing the honourable gentleman
at Greenwich, and I must say, as a workman,
of course, believing Mr. Gladstone's statement
to be true, that he acquitted himself in an
able manner of the truly grave charge that.
rested against him. No doubt the words
spoken at Greenwich on this special subject
remain fresh in the memory of many of your
readers, and, therefore, need no repetition on
my part. But, even 'supposing that it did
rest against Mr.. Gladstone, where can
there be any &nit found, I say, if there was
not sufficient work for the employes?. If such
was the case, the Government were justi-
fied, in justice to the country at large, to
dismiss all superfluous hands, and which must
have been the case' at the very worst. If it
could be proved that the Premier discharged
workmen with the knowledge that they Were
wanted, then I would join ii' myself and de-
nounce such proceedings. But it cannot be
done, and I defy your correspondent to bring
any proofs whatever to support such a charge.
Again, in writing upon the "Seven Points,"
and the Council or " Skilled Workmen," he
find faults with such a title, and calls it a
"snobbish designation." I would ask him wilt
he means by the word f‘ snobbish ? " Does he
mean that it is too laudable a title for such an
assembly as it was supposed to represent ? or does
he mean the contrary, that 'it was not high
enough in its meaning ? a question which he
does not touch upon in his article. Then he
makes use of the following words, that he
felt satisfied "that. it had been created.' by
some of Mr. Gladstone's parasites, in order to
deceive his political opponents, and give him
an opportunity, of sneering at those "—here
habreaks off with what he was going to say,
I presume and leaves the reader in a com-
plete mystification, to rack his brain by think-
ing whom he can possibly mean by "those."
Next comes It grave accusation against Mr.
Scott Russell, that of telling a decided
falsehood; in fact, I infer from the manner in
which that portion of the article is written,
be. is accused of being a principal agent in
what he must think and know to be a
'great political conspiracy. Now these are
rather hard words to Use against any gentle-
man, who might have been sincere, but there
is no occasion to argue the question out, as, to
use the words of Rigby Wason, "there is no
harm done." The most sensible observation
throughout the article is the following:—
"That the great mass of the working classes
are averse to revolutions." ..That I coincide
with R. W. Treat the .British workman
with proper respect—give him that which
is justly due to him—politically and socially,
and he will gratefully appreciate the source
from which such justice should emanate.
I should very much like to read the
pamphlet which It. W. considers his contribu-
tion against the wrOnga. of the working classes,
but I must say if it is written as illogically
as the article I have been bold enough to com-
ment upon, then it does not give its author
much Credit.—l am, &e.,
GEORGE E. TYEEy ,
January 3rd.

PUBLIC-HOUSES.

_
To the Editor of the BEE-HIVE.
am much puzzled to know how it is
that a diminution of the number of persons
to be, in future, licensed to sell intoxicating
liquors, bhould be a question which has caused
strong and violent parties to be organised, and
a Cabinet Minister to suffer defeat. -Until the
existing law is carried out, what need have we
for fresh legislation?
The trade is already an exceptional one,
requiring the person exercising it to obtain a
licence which licence, is given under carefully
framedrestrictions, which, if as carefully out,
would render the houses, in which exoiseable
liquors are sold, places of decent refreshment
for neighbours and travellers. Drunkennes,

in such houses is specially prohibited, and. the
Home Office, through the police, has full
power to prevent drunkenness in any house
kept by a person holding a license.
But 'what I wish specially to bring to the
notice of your readers is, that although every
person applying for •it licence must indicate the
house in which he intends to carry on his
business, and such house must be a fit and
proper place fog, the exercise of this trade,
there is no question, when the license is ap-
plied for, or afterwards, as to who happens to
be the proprietor of such house, and the
persons who grant the licence are, or ought to
be, wholly ignorant of the name of such
proprietor; the licensed seller may live in his
own house, or hire one, the only question is
regarding its fitness. Tam at a loss, therefore,
to know why, if the person licensed relinquishes
his business, or loses his licence for breach of
its tenour, the owner of the house• ihould be
more entitled to compensation than any. "other
person losing a tenant.
If therefore, it is .really wished that the
existing number of public-houses should. be
diminished, magistrates have it in their power
to refuse all new licences and tranfer3 of aid
ones, till the number of licensed persons is
reduced to the required extent; and if it is
wished to prevent drunkenness in the houses
of persons licensed, a direction from the Home
Office to the police to prosecute for all
breaches of the ten= of the licences would
have the desired effect.

The country is about to pay 12 millions for
allowing one law to be broken. There appear
to be persons who Wish to spend an equal sum
to make thing pleasant when another existing
law is to be enforced. • "

Will the Sunday traders in the New Cut
receive compensation in case their trade is
put a stop to by the police? An increase of
our, debt by 21 millions means a perpetual
extra charge Of nearly one million per annum.
—Your obedient servant,
December 30, 1871.

03IICRON.

articles.text:
A PRACTICAL SUGGESTION.—THE
FARM LABOURERS.
To the Editor of the BEE-Ulu. •

Bra, Some of your correspondents
have boldly and clearly pointed out,
to a certain 'extent, the remedy for the ini-
provement of the agricultural labourer.
But the question must be farther pursued.
It is not a question of tenancy, but actual
possession of the land which will be .for a long
time uppermost, and the only solution of the
present difficulty. For, sir, what we have to
contend with is not so much the
.dearth of
this most necessary and special labour but the
source of attraction which is depriving us of
it. It is very necessary that the many who
have thought out this subject should boldly
grapple with it at its root. It is the superior
inducements Which the Western- States of
America, which form the nucleus of agreat
° future agricultural ' ricultural empire are now giving to
the best blood of England and its - greatest
toilers; it is these inducements which natu-
rally have their influence with the owners of
hard hands and willing hearts, and which are
fast depopulating 'the agricultural portions of
England, It is not the towns of England
that Can now be charged, by offering higher
wages for maul:ifs/during purposes, with
emptyingmany a country home, bat Use great
-outflow to America. For in this country of
America an agricultural labourer has land of
'his own immediately that he settles upon it.
His labour pays for it. He has but to settle
down and cultivate the land, and be its owner
in five years. If he has not sufficient to at
once do this le can at present go and earn
it on existing farms at good wages and his
future is very -much. brighter than ;hose .poor
Dorset labourers who have stated their willing-
ness to work at 9s. per week.

To any one cogn-isant of the awful social
life which prevails to a large extent in our
agricultural hamlets and, villages, it is most
painful to witness scenes which must end in
crime and diagram. I was a short time since
in a ;county town, which I forbear to name,
the greater part of which paid rent to the
squire, whose son sits now. in .Parliament for
the county. I went through one lane of
dreadful dwellings, each of which had its pet
cesspool three feet from the hack door, and
each also had a well close to. Fever and
disease invariably reign in this lane; ia fact,
death and . desolation have it all their own
way. There is no trim piece of garden, or any
outlet save the front door. At the end of the
town I stood before a labouring man's cottage
—the cottage of a farm labourer. A heap of
stable manure, which a farmer had shot there,
was in front of the door. The cottage had
two rooms one on the ground, one upstairs—
small holes. The rent was is. 6d. per
week, paid to the squire.. The man's four
children were all afflicted, one was hump-
backed, ono lame, one partly an idot, and the
eldest a terrible specimen of a child, doing
duty at home, whilst father and mother were
at work. This man when in work earned
about ten shillings per week. The vicar of
this place has his thousand a year, and the
squire's income is a fat one. Now these
labourers cannot live on the farm where they

work because the farms have no accommoda-
tion.

Such is a true picture of many parts of
agricultural England. Now, Sir, maintain
there is a remedy—a paying remedy;i that is
if our capitalists will give up to a
i 'aertain ex-
tent foreign loans at high interests, and be
content with five per cent. Let the first man
who wants to try the following remedy set
about it at once. Let him take ten acres of
land, which a steady, firm, and sober labourer
can cultivate himself, and on that build a
four-roomed cottage. Let him supply the
labourer with the necessaries of life to the ex-
tent of the value of £1 per week; and then,
after doing this, let him sell the .protitioe of
the ten acres for one year, and after putting
by his five per cent. interest, ho 'can place the
remainder to the -credit of the labourer as a
fund for him to purchase the freehold.. A
capital cottage can be built for £lOO ; land
has in many instances been sold recently from
£23 to X3O per acre, and the .produce of land
Which a.iitati tills knowing he i 3 Working for
his freehold, will not be either scanty or
below the average. If anyone has £4OO to try
a practical scheme, ,and not a. visionary one,
let him place himself in communication with
me, and the movement will have been com-
menced which will make our labourers in
England ii some sense on an equality with
'their' More fortunate brethren in America.--4
am; Sir, your obedient servant,

,
JOHN PARNELL, '
Author of". Land and Houses."
